title: Little Red Riding Hood: The Deeper Forest
description: Red is 12 years old and brave — but the forest holds more than wolves. A rich, layered journey through trust, manipulation, courage, community, and wisdom. Based on the classic tale, expanded for today's young thinkers.
theme: Trust, critical thinking, resilience, and community
cover_image_prompt: A 12-year-old Indian girl in a bright red hood standing at the edge of a lush magical forest, sunlight filtering through tall trees, a village visible behind her, watercolor storybook style, warm and vibrant, classic fairy tale with Indian village aesthetic
learning_objectives: Recognise manipulation tactics and respond with critical thinking
Understand the difference between trust and blind obedience
See how communities protect each other through honest communication
Practice helping others learn from your own mistakes
learning_concept: Wisdom is not about being fearless — it is about knowing when to trust, when to question, and when to ask for help.
psychological_framework: Social-emotional learning anchored in trust calibration, bystander effect awareness, and post-traumatic growth theory

ai_image_config.style: watercolor storybook illustration, warm village and forest setting, classic fairy tale aesthetic with Indian-inspired village details, soft pastel tones, age 10-15 friendly

chapters.title: The Journey Begins
chapters.teaser: Grandmother is waiting. The forest path is familiar. But something feels different today.

chapters.title: The Wolf's Cunning
chapters.teaser: He has a gentle voice, a warm smile — and every answer feels just a little too smooth.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Cottage
chapters.teaser: Something is wrong inside. Red knows it. But proving it is harder than feeling it.

chapters.title: The Reckoning
chapters.teaser: Standing up is terrifying. But staying silent has its own cost.

chapters.title: The Aftermath
chapters.teaser: The wolf is gone — but the feelings he left behind need to be talked about.

chapters.title: A New Friend
chapters.teaser: Priya wants to be friends. After everything that happened, can Red trust again?

chapters.title: The Village Rumour
chapters.teaser: People are saying things about Red that are not quite true. What do you do?

chapters.title: The Second Forest
chapters.teaser: Little sister Meera wants to go through the forest alone. Red must decide how to guide her.

chapters.title: The Wolf Returns
chapters.teaser: The wolf has a new trick — and this time he is targeting the whole village.

chapters.title: Wisdom's Harvest
chapters.teaser: Red speaks at the school assembly. What will she tell them? What did it all mean?

scenes.title: The Familiar Path
scenes.narrative: Red pulls her bright hood tight and steps onto the forest path for what feels like the hundredth time. Grandmother's cottage is just three kilometres through the trees, and her basket is heavy with fresh roti, mango pickle, and the herbal medicine Mother packed last night. The forest smells of earth and rain, and the birds are loud and cheerful above her head. She has made this journey a dozen times before — but today, something in the air makes her pause at the tree line and think before stepping in.
scenes.image_prompt: A 12-year-old Indian girl in a red hood pausing at the edge of a lush forest, morning sunlight, basket on her arm, looking thoughtfully at the path ahead, Indian village visible behind her, warm watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Pausing to think before acting — even when something feels familiar — is a sign of growing wisdom, not fear.

choices.label: Stick to the main path and walk quickly — you know this forest well
choices.description: Confidence in familiar ground. Speed and routine.

choices.label: Tell Mother exactly which path you are taking and when to expect you back
choices.description: Letting trusted adults know your plans is a smart habit.

scenes.title: Distracted by Flowers
scenes.narrative: About halfway through the forest, Red spots a stunning cluster of wild marigolds just off the path — exactly the kind Grandmother loves. She could pick a small bunch and it would take only a few minutes. But she also remembers Mother's words: 'Stay on the path, do not dally.' The flowers are beautiful. The detour is small. And yet she finds herself thinking about whether small deviations from a plan are ever really small.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood standing on a forest path, eyeing a beautiful cluster of wild marigolds just off the trail, golden afternoon light, thoughtful expression, watercolor storybook style with warm forest tones
scenes.coaching_moment: Instructions from people who care about us are not just rules — they are often the result of someone thinking further ahead than we are.

choices.label: Pick a small bunch quickly and then stick to the path — Grandmother will love them
choices.description: A small joy — but a deviation from the plan.

choices.label: Leave the flowers and keep walking — instructions matter for a reason
choices.description: Discipline and respect for guidance.

scenes.title: The Sound in the Undergrowth
scenes.narrative: Red hears a rustling in the undergrowth about ten metres to her left. It is loud — too loud for a bird, too slow for a deer. She stops walking and listens. The rustling stops. She takes two more steps. The rustling starts again, keeping pace with her. Her heart rate rises. She thinks of running, but running means turning her back. She thinks of calling out, but she does not know who — or what — is listening.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood frozen on a forest path, tense and alert, dark undergrowth on either side, sunlight through tall trees above, eerie stillness, watercolor storybook illustration with a slightly mysterious mood
scenes.coaching_moment: When something feels wrong, trusting that feeling is the first step — the second step is what you do with it.

choices.label: Walk faster and stay alert — reach Grandmother's cottage as quickly as possible
choices.description: Move toward safety. Stay focused on the destination.

choices.label: Stop and call out loudly: 'I know someone is there. I am not afraid.'
choices.description: Assert yourself. Sometimes naming the fear takes its power away.

scenes.title: A Polite Stranger
scenes.narrative: He steps out from behind an oak tree as if he just happened to be passing by — a tall man with a friendly smile and an easy, comfortable voice. He introduces himself simply as 'a traveller' who knows these woods very well. He asks where Red is going. His voice is warm. His eyes are bright. And yet something about the way he asks — leaning slightly forward, paying very close attention to her answer — gives Red a cold, prickling feeling at the back of her neck.
scenes.image_prompt: A charming but slightly unsettling stranger speaking to a girl in a red hood on a forest path, the stranger's smile seems a little too wide, dappled forest light, watercolor storybook illustration, Indian forest setting
scenes.coaching_moment: Manipulation does not always look threatening — it often looks friendly, warm, and reasonable. That is what makes it so important to notice.

choices.label: Answer vaguely: 'Just visiting a relative nearby' — don't give details to strangers
choices.description: Protect information. Be polite but not specific.

choices.label: Tell him the truth — he seems kind and maybe he can walk you there
choices.description: Openness, but at a cost of caution.

scenes.title: Flattery and Pressure
scenes.narrative: The stranger begins to compliment Red — her cleverness, her bravery for walking the forest alone, how mature she seems for her age. Each compliment lands softly, but together they feel like a net being slowly pulled closed. He suggests a shortcut through the 'deep grove' that would save thirty minutes. 'Clever girls like you don't need to follow boring old paths,' he says, with a smile. Red notices that he keeps using her own desire to seem mature against her. She has seen this technique before — in a school lesson about persuasion.
scenes.image_prompt: A stranger gesturing toward a darker path in the forest while a girl in red looks thoughtful and slightly suspicious, afternoon light, the dark path looks mysterious, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: When someone uses your desire to seem smart or brave as a tool to make you do what they want, that is a form of manipulation called flattery pressure — and recognising it is a superpower.

choices.label: Thank him politely but stick to your original path — 'I know this way works'
choices.description: Hold your ground with politeness. You do not need to be rude to say no.

choices.label: Say you need to think about it and ask him to wait while you decide
choices.description: Delay decisions under pressure to think more clearly.

scenes.title: He Disappears
scenes.narrative: The stranger's expression shifts — just briefly, just a flicker — when Red refuses to take the shortcut. He says something about needing to continue his own journey and walks away into the trees. Red watches him go. He does not walk like someone who was just passing through. He walks with purpose, directly and fast, in the direction of Grandmother's cottage. Red feels a cold knot of dread settle in her stomach. She needs to make a decision, and she needs to make it quickly.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood watching a stranger walk away purposefully into deep forest shadows, her expression showing realisation and concern, urgent forest atmosphere, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: When something feels wrong even after you have done the right thing, that feeling is worth listening to — it is your instincts giving you important information.

choices.label: Run as fast as you can to Grandmother's cottage — every second counts now
choices.description: React to the threat with urgency and speed.

choices.label: Stop at the forest edge and shout for the woodcutter — there is safety in alerting others
choices.description: Ask for help before running into possible danger alone.

scenes.title: Something Is Wrong
scenes.narrative: Grandmother's cottage looks the same from outside — blue painted door, the old tulsi plant by the step, the clay pots on the windowsill. But it smells different. Not of cardamom and dal, which is what it always smells like. It smells of the outdoors, of someone who has walked far and sweated in the heat. The door is slightly open. And when Red calls 'Grandmother?' the voice that answers sounds like Grandmother — but only almost. Like a recording that is slightly out of tune.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood standing at the door of a cosy cottage looking suspicious and cautious, the door is slightly ajar, warm but unsettling atmosphere, watercolor storybook illustration with Indian cottage details
scenes.coaching_moment: Sometimes the most important information is not what you see but what you sense — small mismatches between what should be and what is.

choices.label: Enter slowly and keep your eyes wide open — notice every detail that is out of place
choices.description: Cautious investigation. Keep your guard up.

choices.label: Ask through the door: 'Grandmother, what did you make for dinner last Tuesday?'
choices.description: Test the voice with a question only Grandmother would know.

scenes.title: Inside the Cottage
scenes.narrative: Inside, Grandmother is in her chair — but she is sitting too still, her eyes too bright, her smile slightly frozen. The stranger is gone but his presence is everywhere: a muddy bootprint by the door, a cup of tea left half-drunk on the table, a window pushed open from inside. Grandmother whispers urgently: 'Red. He was here. He left when he heard you coming. I told him nothing, but he knows your name.' The familiar warmth of the cottage feels dangerous now. Red has to decide what to do next.
scenes.image_prompt: Inside a warm cottage, an elderly Indian woman in a chair looking frightened but composed, a girl in a red hood crouched beside her, muddy bootprint on the floor visible, urgent atmosphere, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: When someone you love is in danger, the most helpful thing is not to panic — it is to be calm enough to think clearly and act wisely.

choices.label: Stay with Grandmother and bolt the door — safety first, then plan
choices.description: Secure the situation before taking further action.

choices.label: Help Grandmother out through the back window and get her to safety
choices.description: Move her away from the threat entirely.

scenes.title: The Woodcutter Arrives
scenes.narrative: There is a knock at the door. A deep, familiar voice: 'Hello? I am Priya's father — I was checking on Meena-ji on my way back from the timber yard.' Red takes a breath. She looks at Grandmother. They exchange a glance that says: this is someone safe. This is someone who can help. But Red still hesitates — she has been manipulated once today by someone who seemed trustworthy. She must decide how much to share and how quickly.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood and an elderly woman exchanging a glance at a bolted cottage door as someone knocks from outside, cautious but hopeful expressions, warm firelight, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: After being deceived, caution is healthy — but caution that prevents you from accepting genuine help can become its own problem. Learning to tell the difference is wisdom.

choices.label: Open the door and explain everything — the woodcutter can help protect you both
choices.description: Accept help from a trustworthy adult in the community.

choices.label: Ask him to go alert Mr. Fernandes, the Village Elder, while you stay with Grandmother
choices.description: Coordinate a community response before opening up.

scenes.title: Face to Face
scenes.narrative: The wolf — for now everyone knows that is what he is — is found at the edge of the village, trying to talk his way into another home. He spots Red and his expression changes: something cold and calculating where the warmth used to be. He tries a final tactic: 'You are a brave girl. Too brave. Bravery without proof gets people into trouble.' He is trying to make her doubt herself. Mr. Fernandes, the Village Elder, stands behind Red and waits to see what she does.
scenes.image_prompt: A 12-year-old girl in a red hood standing her ground in front of a manipulative adult man at a village edge, an elder watching from behind her, strong composition showing courage vs. manipulation, warm watercolor storybook style
scenes.coaching_moment: When someone tries to make you doubt yourself as a way to silence you, that is itself evidence that you are right to speak up.

choices.label: Speak clearly: 'I have evidence. I will share it with Mr. Fernandes right now.'
choices.description: Calm, evidenced assertion. No anger needed.

choices.label: Step aside and let Mr. Fernandes ask the questions — he has more authority
choices.description: Use the right person for the right moment.

scenes.title: The Evidence
scenes.narrative: Red reaches into her basket and produces the one thing she almost did not bring: the small notebook where she writes her observations. In it, under today's date, she has written: 'Stranger on the path. Tall. Scar on left hand. Said he was a traveller but walked like someone who knew exactly where he was going.' The muddy bootprint at Grandmother's cottage matches the boot of the man standing in front of them. Mr. Fernandes looks at the note. He looks at the man. The man runs.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood holding up a small notebook as evidence, a village elder and community members looking at it, the wolf fleeing in the background, triumphant but still tense atmosphere, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Keeping notes and paying attention to details is not just a school skill — it is a life skill that can protect you and the people you love.

choices.label: Ask the villagers to spread out and watch the forest paths so he cannot return
choices.description: Organise a community response — think beyond just yourself.

choices.label: Go back to Grandmother immediately — she needs you more than the chase does
choices.description: Priorities: your people come before the pursuit.

scenes.title: The Village Gathers
scenes.narrative: By evening, the village has gathered at the central well to talk about what happened. Red sits beside Grandmother, who holds her hand and says nothing for a long time. Then she says: 'I was frightened too. But watching you today reminded me what courage actually looks like — not having no fear, but deciding to act anyway.' Mr. Fernandes asks Red to describe exactly what she noticed about the stranger, so the whole village can learn to recognise the same warning signs.
scenes.image_prompt: A warm village gathering at a central well at dusk, an Indian girl in a red hood speaking to a group of attentive villagers, her grandmother beside her, community and warmth, soft watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Real courage is not the absence of fear — it is the decision to do the right thing even while you feel afraid.

choices.label: Share everything you observed in detail — the more people know, the safer everyone is
choices.description: Community safety through shared knowledge.

choices.label: Ask Mr. Fernandes to lead the discussion — you will add details when asked
choices.description: Collaborative leadership. You do not have to carry this alone.

scenes.title: A Sleepless Night
scenes.narrative: That night, Red cannot sleep. She keeps replaying the moments on the path — should she have shouted earlier? Run faster? Not gone at all? The thoughts circle and circle without landing anywhere helpful. Mother comes in and sits on the edge of the bed, and Red finds herself telling her everything: not just what happened, but what she felt and thought during it. Something about saying the feelings out loud makes them slightly less heavy.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood sitting up in bed at night, unable to sleep, her mother sitting beside her listening with care, soft moonlight through a window, warm and gentle watercolor illustration, Indian home setting
scenes.coaching_moment: After a frightening experience, talking about it — really talking, including the feelings — is not weakness. It is how our minds begin to heal.

choices.label: Tell Mother everything, including the scary thoughts you are having at night
choices.description: Full honesty with a trusted adult helps process the experience.

choices.label: Tell Mother the facts but keep the scary feelings private — you do not want to worry her
choices.description: Protective instinct, but it carries the weight alone.

scenes.title: Grandmother's Wisdom
scenes.narrative: Two days later, Red visits Grandmother, who is making tea and seems entirely herself again. Grandmother says: 'The man counted on you being too embarrassed to tell people. He counted on you thinking no one would believe you. That is how people like that survive — by convincing you that your feelings are not worth trusting.' Red asks: 'How do you stop being afraid after something like that?' Grandmother puts down her cup and looks at her granddaughter for a long time before answering.
scenes.image_prompt: An elderly Indian woman and a young girl in a red hood sitting together over cups of tea, a wise and warm conversation, sunlight through cottage windows, watercolor storybook illustration with warmth and healing
scenes.coaching_moment: Processing an experience with someone wise and safe — a grandparent, a counsellor, a trusted elder — is one of the most important things you can do after something frightening.

choices.label: Ask Grandmother: 'How did you stay calm when he was there?'
choices.description: Learn from her experience and model her resilience.

choices.label: Tell Grandmother: 'I feel guilty. Maybe I should have run faster.'
choices.description: Share the self-blame, which is common after difficult experiences.

scenes.title: Writing It Down
scenes.narrative: Mr. Fernandes visits to check on Grandmother and brings Red a gift: a new notebook — larger than the old one, with thick cream pages. 'For your next set of observations,' he says with a smile. He tells Red that because of her quick thinking and detailed notes, two other families have come forward to say the stranger had tried the same approach with their children the previous week. 'Your courage did not just protect you,' he says. 'It protected them too.' Red opens the new notebook and writes the date at the top of the first page.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood opening a new notebook gifted by a kind village elder, sitting in a bright cottage with her grandmother and a warm community figure, sense of closure and new beginning, watercolor illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: When you speak up about something difficult, you often discover that others experienced the same thing but felt too alone to say so. Your voice can give others permission to use theirs.

choices.label: Write a summary of what you learned about manipulation tactics — to remember and to share
choices.description: Convert experience into transferable knowledge.

choices.label: Write a note of thanks to all the people who helped — Grandmother, the Woodcutter, Mr. Fernandes
choices.description: Gratitude as a practice of acknowledging what community means.

scenes.title: Priya Knocks
scenes.narrative: A week passes. One afternoon, there is a knock at Red's door. It is Priya — the woodcutter's daughter, who is Red's age and has lived two lanes away for years without them ever really speaking. She holds out a small parcel: her mother sent extra sesame laddus as a thank-you for Red's help. Priya has kind eyes and an open face. She says: 'I know what happened to you in the forest. I am sorry. I also know you are very brave.' Red looks at her and feels two things at once: warmth and caution.
scenes.image_prompt: Two girls of similar age at a doorway, one holding a parcel of sweets, both looking at each other with warmth and slight uncertainty, Indian village setting, afternoon light, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: After a difficult experience, it is natural to be more careful with trust — and it is also important not to let that caution cut you off from new friendships that are genuinely good.

choices.label: Invite Priya in — offer her tea and begin to get to know her properly
choices.description: Open a door to genuine connection.

choices.label: Thank her warmly but keep things brief — you are not ready to let new people in yet
choices.description: Honest about your current state without being rude.

scenes.title: Testing Trust
scenes.narrative: Over the following days, Red and Priya meet several times. Priya is thoughtful, funny, and genuinely curious about people. But one afternoon, Priya says something that bothers Red: 'I heard your mother was really angry at you for going into the forest after what happened. Is that true?' The information is wrong — Mother was not angry at all. And Red is not sure where Priya heard it. She could have made it up, or she could have heard it from someone who got the story confused.
scenes.image_prompt: Two girls walking together in a village lane, one looking slightly troubled by something the other has said, bright afternoon atmosphere, Indian village setting, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Good friendships can handle honest questions. If something bothers you about a new friend, addressing it directly — kindly — is better than letting it silently erode the trust.

choices.label: Ask Priya directly: 'That is not right — where did you hear that?'
choices.description: Gentle confrontation. Test the friendship with honesty.

choices.label: Say nothing for now — wait and watch to see if Priya is trustworthy over time
choices.description: Patient observation before judgement.

scenes.title: Real Friends
scenes.narrative: Priya listens to Red's correction, looks embarrassed, and says: 'I heard it from Tara who heard it from someone else. I should have asked you directly instead of repeating it. I am sorry.' It is a genuine apology — quick, clean, and with no excuses. Red looks at her new friend and notices something: a person who gets it wrong but corrects themselves without making it a big production is often more trustworthy than someone who claims never to make mistakes at all. She smiles. 'Let us start again properly,' she says.
scenes.image_prompt: Two girls smiling at each other in a sunny courtyard, one having just apologised, warmth and new connection, Indian village setting with bright flowers, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Trustworthy people are not people who never make mistakes — they are people who own their mistakes and do not repeat them.

choices.label: Forgive Priya fully and invite her to walk to Grandmother's cottage together
choices.description: Extend genuine trust to someone who has earned it.

choices.label: Forgive her, but privately decide to wait a little longer before trusting her with big things
choices.description: Calibrated trust: forgiveness and caution can coexist.

scenes.title: What People Are Saying
scenes.narrative: Red is at the market with Priya when she overhears two women talking about her. The story they are telling is not quite right: in their version, Red panicked, screamed, and had to be rescued by the woodcutter. In reality, Red stayed calm, gathered evidence, and helped coordinate the village response. Red's first instinct is anger. Her second — once she breathes — is curiosity about how the story got so distorted, and what to do about it.
scenes.image_prompt: Two girls at a colourful Indian village market, one of them overhearing nearby women telling an inaccurate story, expression shifting from surprise to composed thoughtfulness, warm busy market atmosphere, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Rumours often start not from malice but from incomplete information passed through many people — each adding their own assumptions. Understanding this can turn anger into strategy.

choices.label: Approach the women politely and correct the record: 'Actually, this is what happened...'
choices.description: Direct, calm correction of false information.

choices.label: Leave it — the story does not really hurt anyone and correcting strangers is awkward
choices.description: Avoid the conflict, but the inaccurate story persists.

scenes.title: A Friend Defends
scenes.narrative: At school the next day, Red discovers that the rumour has spread further — and now a version is circulating that says Red invented the whole wolf story because she broke something at Grandmother's house and wanted an excuse. It is absurd. It is hurtful. And Red overhears a group of classmates laughing about it near the water tap. Priya, who is standing next to Red, looks at the group and then at Red. She clearly wants to say something on Red's behalf, but waits to check what Red wants first.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood and her friend standing in a school courtyard, a group of classmates laughing nearby, the friend looking at the protagonist asking permission to speak up, Indian school setting, watercolor illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: A friend who checks what you need before charging into a situation on your behalf is showing the best kind of support — strength combined with respect.

choices.label: Tell Priya: 'Go ahead — tell them the truth. I will back you up.'
choices.description: Let a friend help. That is what friendship is for.

choices.label: Tell Priya: 'Leave it. I will write the real story down and give it to Mr. Fernandes to read at assembly.'
choices.description: Use the formal channel. Fight misinformation with documentation.

scenes.title: Standing in the Truth
scenes.narrative: Whether through Priya's direct challenge in the courtyard or through Mr. Fernandes reading Red's written account at assembly, the rumour begins to collapse under the weight of actual facts. One of the classmates who was laughing earlier comes up to Red privately and says: 'I am sorry. I did not know the real story. I should not have assumed.' Red looks at him — a boy who had the small courage to come and say this when no one made him — and finds she is not as angry as she expected.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood accepting a quiet apology from a classmate at the edge of a school courtyard, surprised but open expression, afternoon light, warm watercolor storybook illustration of a reconciliation moment
scenes.coaching_moment: Accepting an honest apology is an act of courage too — it closes a loop that staying angry would keep spinning forever.

choices.label: Accept the apology warmly and move on — the truth has done its work
choices.description: Gracious resolution. The cycle ends here.

choices.label: Accept the apology and ask him: 'What made you question the rumour?'
choices.description: Learn from his reasoning — useful for the future.

scenes.title: Meera's Request
scenes.narrative: It is a bright Saturday when eight-year-old Meera comes to Red with shining eyes and an enormous idea. She wants to walk through the forest to pick wildflowers for Mother's birthday — alone, like Red used to do. 'You went all the time when you were my age,' Meera says, which is true. Red crouches down and looks at her little sister. She thinks about everything she now knows. She does not want to frighten Meera or take her freedom away. But she also knows what she did not know before.
scenes.image_prompt: An older girl in a red hood crouching down to speak to her excited 8-year-old little sister outside their home, a forest visible in the distance, tender and serious expression, warm watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Guiding someone younger than you is not about saying no — it is about helping them be ready for what they will face. The goal is to expand their safety, not shrink their world.

choices.label: Offer to come with her — make it an adventure for both of you, together
choices.description: Protect and share the experience. Go together.

choices.label: Agree she can go — but first teach her three rules you wish you had known
choices.description: Empower her with knowledge before she goes.

scenes.title: Meera Meets a Stranger
scenes.narrative: Whether they walk together or Meera walks with Red's rules in her heart, the same thing happens: a stranger at the edge of the forest offers to show Meera 'a shortcut to the prettiest flowers.' The man seems kind. He has a bright smile. Meera looks at him and then — in a moment that makes Red's heart leap — Meera says: 'No thank you. I already know where the flowers are.' The man's smile flickers. He shrugs and walks away. Meera looks at Red and says: 'Was that him?'
scenes.image_prompt: A young girl confidently declining a stranger's offer at a forest edge while her older sister watches proudly from nearby, the stranger looking mildly surprised, watercolor storybook illustration with a triumphant mood
scenes.coaching_moment: The greatest gift you can give someone younger is not protection — it is the knowledge that lets them protect themselves.

choices.label: Tell Meera: 'I do not know. But you did exactly the right thing. I am so proud of you.'
choices.description: Reinforce the correct behaviour with specific, warm praise.

choices.label: Report the man to Mr. Fernandes immediately — if it is not the wolf, it is someone like him
choices.description: Escalate to community protection again. Patterns matter.

scenes.title: Teaching What You Know
scenes.narrative: On the walk home, Meera holds Red's hand and says: 'How did you know to teach me those things?' Red thinks about it carefully before answering. She thinks about the lessons she learned the hard way — about flattery as a trap, about how something wrong can feel normal if you are not watching carefully. She tells Meera: 'Because someone should have taught me, and they did not, and I do not want that for you.' Meera squeezes her hand. The flowers for Mother are safely in the basket.
scenes.image_prompt: Two sisters walking home through a sunlit Indian village, older sister holding younger sister's hand, a basket of wildflowers, warm golden afternoon light, watercolor storybook illustration of tender sibling bond
scenes.coaching_moment: One of the most powerful things about learning hard lessons is the opportunity to pass on what you know — before someone else has to learn it the same hard way.

choices.label: Tell Meera: 'Never be embarrassed to ask for help — that is what the community is for'
choices.description: Leave her with the most important lesson about seeking help.

choices.label: Tell Meera: 'Keep a notebook. Observations are how you stay safe and tell the truth.'
choices.description: Pass on the practical habit that protected you.

scenes.title: A New Trick
scenes.narrative: The wolf is back — but this time he has not come to the forest. He has come to the village itself, presenting himself as a travelling merchant selling protective amulets 'against wolves and bad fortune.' His prices are very low. His charm is very high. Several families have already bought from him, and he is now asking if he can give a 'safety talk' to the children at the village school. Mr. Fernandes is uncertain — the merchant has seemed helpful so far. Red recognises him immediately. But no one else does.
scenes.image_prompt: A disguised wolf-like figure presenting himself as a charming merchant in a village square, families around him, a girl in a red hood watching from the edge of the crowd with recognition on her face, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Manipulation changes its costume but rarely its methods. Recognising patterns — even in new situations — is one of the most important skills you can develop.

choices.label: Go to Mr. Fernandes immediately and tell him: 'I know this man. I need to show you something.'
choices.description: Act on what you know through the proper channel.

choices.label: Find Priya first — make sure you have a witness before making a serious accusation
choices.description: Careful preparation before a public claim.

scenes.title: The Community Tests Him
scenes.narrative: Mr. Fernandes listens to Red. He does not dismiss her. He does not say 'Are you sure?' with that tone that means 'I do not believe you.' He calls a quiet meeting of five trusted villagers and together they design a test: they will ask the merchant specific questions that only a genuine trader would know. Red helps design the questions. The merchant struggles badly. His amulets are worthless. His story has too many gaps. The community works together, quietly and effectively, to expose him without a confrontation.
scenes.image_prompt: A village elder and a girl in a red hood planning together with four other trusted community members around a table, strategic and focused expressions, warm lamplight, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: The strongest protection is not individual bravery — it is a community that trusts each other enough to work together thoughtfully when a threat appears.

choices.label: Let Mr. Fernandes lead the questioning — you watch and document the results
choices.description: Support the process from a position of quiet strength.

choices.label: Ask to ask the merchant one question directly — something only the real wolf would react to
choices.description: Direct, personal confrontation with a specific memory.

scenes.title: He Leaves — For Good
scenes.narrative: The merchant is escorted to the edge of the village and told clearly that he is not welcome in this community. He does not run this time — there is no point. He walks. But as he passes Red, he says quietly: 'You have a good memory, girl.' Red looks at him without flinching. 'Yes,' she says. 'I do.' He leaves. The village watches him go together. Priya puts her arm around Red's shoulder. Grandmother, who walked out of her cottage to watch, says nothing — just nods, once, with a smile that Red will remember for the rest of her life.
scenes.image_prompt: A whole village watching a merchant-disguised figure leave at the village boundary, a girl in a red hood at the front with her head high, community around her, Grandmother nodding from her doorway, watercolor storybook illustration, triumphant atmosphere
scenes.coaching_moment: A community that has learned to trust itself — and the honest voices within it — is one of the most powerful forces in the world.

choices.label: Celebrate quietly with Priya and Grandmother — some victories deserve a small, private joy
choices.description: Savour the moment with the people who matter most.

choices.label: Begin planning with Mr. Fernandes: what can the village do to prevent this from happening again?
choices.description: Turn the win into lasting change.

scenes.title: The Assembly Invitation
scenes.narrative: Three weeks later, Mr. Fernandes comes to Red's home with an unusual request. The school headmistress has asked if Red would speak at the morning assembly — not about the wolf specifically, but about what she learned. 'About trust, about recognising manipulation, about asking for help,' Mr. Fernandes says. 'Things every child in that school needs to hear, from someone their own age who actually lived through it.' Red sits with the invitation and thinks. She is not afraid, exactly. But this is different from being brave in a moment. This is choosing to be open.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood sitting at a table with a school assembly invitation in front of her, thinking carefully, warm home setting with afternoon light, watercolor storybook illustration, thoughtful and poised
scenes.coaching_moment: Sharing what you have learned — especially the hard lessons — is a generous act. It says: I went through this so that others might go through it less alone.

choices.label: Accept immediately — this is exactly the kind of thing you have been preparing for
choices.description: Full commitment. The experience has made you ready.

choices.label: Accept, but ask if Priya can stand beside you on stage — you are braver together
choices.description: Courage in community. You do not have to stand alone.

scenes.title: Writing the Speech
scenes.narrative: That evening, Red opens her notebook and begins to write what she wants to say. She writes: 'I used to think bravery meant not being afraid. I now know it means being afraid and acting anyway.' She writes about the forest, the flattery, the cold knot in her stomach. She writes about Grandmother's wisdom, about Priya's honesty, about Mr. Fernandes' patience. She writes about Meera and the flowers. When she is done, she reads it back. It is not a story about a wolf. It is a story about learning to trust yourself — and the right people around you.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood writing carefully in a notebook by candlelight, pages spread around her, warm evening light, focused and purposeful expression, watercolor storybook illustration
scenes.coaching_moment: Writing down what you have learned is how scattered experience becomes wisdom — usable, shareable, and real.

choices.label: Focus the speech on the practical skills: notice the warning signs, ask for help, trust your instincts
choices.description: Give others the tools you wish you had had.

choices.label: Focus on the emotional truth: it is okay to be afraid, and it is okay to need help
choices.description: Give others permission to be vulnerable. That is its own power.

scenes.title: Full Circle
scenes.narrative: Red stands before the school assembly. Four hundred students, forty teachers, and in the back row — Grandmother, the woodcutter, Priya, Mr. Fernandes, and Meera, who is clutching a small bunch of wildflowers and beaming. Red takes a breath. She begins: 'My name is Red. You probably know a story about me — probably not the true one. Here is the true one.' When she finishes, the silence lasts three long seconds. Then comes the applause — not the polite kind, but the kind that means something. Meera's wildflowers end up on the stage.
scenes.image_prompt: A girl in a red hood speaking confidently at a school assembly stage, hundreds of students listening, friends and grandmother in the back row, wildflowers on the stage, triumphant and warm watercolor storybook illustration, full circle moment
scenes.coaching_moment: A story that ends with you teaching others what you learned is the best kind of ending — because it means the story is still going.

choices.label: End with the words: 'Ask for help. The community is your strength.'
choices.description: Centre the community — because no one succeeds alone.
choices.ending_message: Red's story rippled through the village like a stone through still water. Three children came forward after the assembly to share similar experiences they had been too afraid to mention. Meera grew up to teach safety workshops at schools across the district. And Red? She kept writing in her notebooks — observation by observation, lesson by lesson — long into a life full of courage, wisdom, and the best kind of trust.

choices.label: End with: 'Trust yourself. Your instincts are worth listening to.'
choices.description: Centre the individual — because self-trust is where it all begins.
choices.ending_message: Red stood on that stage and gave every child in the hall something they would carry far longer than any lesson from a textbook: the knowledge that their own instincts matter, that their voice counts, and that a story lived honestly — even one that begins with fear — can end with wisdom. Grandmother wiped her eyes in the back row and said nothing. She did not need to.

glossary_terms.definition: When someone tries to influence you in a sneaky or unfair way, often by using your own feelings or desires against you.
Carefully examining information or a situation before deciding what to believe or do, rather than just accepting things at face value.
The idea that some people who are unfamiliar to you may not be safe, and that being cautious with strangers is wise.
A story or piece of information that spreads from person to person but may not be accurate or true.
Believing that someone is reliable, honest, and safe — something that is built slowly over time through consistent actions.
The ability to understand and share how another person is feeling, even when their experience is different from yours.
The feeling that you should do something because the people around you are doing it or expect it of you.
A group of people who live near each other or share something in common and look out for one another.
The ability to recover and adapt after something difficult or frightening has happened.
Knowledge and good judgement that comes from experience, reflection, and learning from mistakes.
Doing something important and right even when you feel afraid — not the absence of fear, but acting despite it.
A person or group who has the power or responsibility to make decisions and help keep people safe.
Giving clear and willing permission for something to happen — and the right to say no if you do not want it.
Talking about other people's private affairs, often based on incomplete information and usually not helpful to anyone.
Thinking carefully and honestly about your own thoughts, feelings, and actions — especially after something significant.
Giving someone excessive compliments, often to get something from them or to make them lower their guard.

coaching_moment: Wisdom is not about being fearless — it is about knowing when to trust, when to question, and when to ask for help.
reflection_prompt: Looking back at the choices you made, which one felt hardest and why? What would you do differently if you replayed?
